metadata.title: Efficient Decision-Making by Volume-Conserving Physical Object

extraction_notes.note: The paper has no section headings before the Acknowledgement, so every node has an empty section; two equations share the label eq:cond1 (Eqs. 6 and 7).
Typos in the source kept verbatim: E(S) = (mu_A + mu_B) N should be a difference; N_N stands for N_B.
Table 1 (the per-machine estimates used in Eqs. 11-12) is a table, not a fact; its entries are only referenced by DP5.
TOW dynamics is typed algorithm with origin external (Kim et al.), although the conclusion says 'we proposed TOW dynamics'; the same authors introduced it in the cited prior work.

nodes.name: Superior performance of TOW dynamics (prior work)
nodes.statement: In our previous studies~\cite{kim1,kim2,kim3,kim4,kim5,kim6}, we showed that, owing to the nonlocal correlation derived from the volume-conservation law, TOW dynamics exhibit higher performance than other well-known algorithms such as the modified $\epsilon$-greedy algorithm and the modified softmax algorithm, which is comparable to the UCB1-tuned algorithm (seen as the best choice among parameter-free algorithms~\cite{auer}).
nodes.statement_short: TOW dynamics outperform modified epsilon-greedy and softmax and match UCB1-tuned, owing to volume conservation.

nodes.name: Multi-armed bandit problem (MBP)
nodes.statement: Suppose there are $M$ slot machines, each of which returns a reward; for example, a coin, with a certain probability that is unknown to a player. Let us consider a minimal case: two machines A and B give rewards with individual probabilities $P_A$ and $P_B$, respectively. The player makes a decision on which machine to play at each trial, trying to maximize the total reward obtained after repeating several trials. The multi-armed bandit problem (MBP) is used to determine the optimal strategy for finding the machine with the highest reward probability as accurately and quickly as possible by referring to past experiences.
nodes.statement_short: Choose among slot machines with unknown reward probabilities to find the best machine quickly and accurately, maximizing total reward.

nodes.name: Tug-of-war (TOW) dynamics
nodes.statement: Consider a volume-conserving physical object; for example, a rigid body like an iron bar (the slot-machine's handle), as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:stow}. Here, the variable $X_k$ represents the displacement of terminal $k$ from an initial position, where $k\in \{A,B\}$. If $X_k$ is a maximum, we assume that the body makes a decision to play machine $k$. In TOW dynamics, the MBP is represented in its inverse form: instead of ``rewarding'' the player when machine $k$ produces a coin with a probability $P_k$, we ``punish'' the player when the machine gives no coin with a probability $1 - P_k$. In this respect, the displacement $X_A$ ($= - X_B$) is determined by the following equations: \begin{eqnarray} X_A(t) & = & Q_A(t) - Q_B(t) + \delta(t) ,\\ Q_k(t) & = & N_k - (1 + \omega)\hspace{1mm}L_k . \end{eqnarray} Here, $Q_k(t)$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) is an ``estimate'' of information on past experiences accumulated from the initial time $1$ to current time $t$, $N_k$ counts the number of times that machine $k$ has been played, $L_k$ counts the number of punishments when playing machine $k$, $\delta(t)$ is an arbitrary fluctuation to which the body is subjected, and $\omega$ is a weighting parameter to be described in detail later on in this Letter. Eq.(\ref{eq:org}), called the ``learning rule'', reflects the volume-conservation law. Consequently the TOW dynamics evolve according to a particularly simple rule: in addition to the fluctuation, if machine $k$ is played at each time $t$, $+1$ and $-\omega$ are added to $X_k(t-1)$ when rewarded and non-rewarded, respectively (Fig.~\ref{fig:stow}).
nodes.statement_short: Play the machine whose terminal displacement $X_k$ is maximal; update $X_A=Q_A-Q_B+\delta$ with $Q_k=N_k-(1+\omega)L_k$.
input: the variable $X_k$ represents the displacement of terminal $k$ from an initial position, where $k\in \{A,B\}$

nodes.name: Decide by maximal displacement
nodes.statement: If $X_k$ is a maximum, we assume that the body makes a decision to play machine $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Play the machine whose displacement is largest.

nodes.name: Compute displacement from estimates
nodes.statement: In this respect, the displacement $X_A$ ($= - X_B$) is determined by the following equations: \begin{eqnarray} X_A(t) & = & Q_A(t) - Q_B(t) + \delta(t) ,\\ Q_k(t) & = & N_k - (1 + \omega)\hspace{1mm}L_k . \end{eqnarray} Here, $Q_k(t)$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) is an ``estimate'' of information on past experiences accumulated from the initial time $1$ to current time $t$, $N_k$ counts the number of times that machine $k$ has been played, $L_k$ counts the number of punishments when playing machine $k$, $\delta(t)$ is an arbitrary fluctuation to which the body is subjected, and $\omega$ is a weighting parameter to be described in detail later on in this Letter.
nodes.statement_short: Displacement is the difference of the two learning-rule estimates plus a fluctuation.

nodes.name: Learning rule
nodes.statement: Eq.(\ref{eq:org}), called the ``learning rule'', reflects the volume-conservation law.

nodes.name: Update terminal on reward or punishment
nodes.statement: Consequently the TOW dynamics evolve according to a particularly simple rule: in addition to the fluctuation, if machine $k$ is played at each time $t$, $+1$ and $-\omega$ are added to $X_k(t-1)$ when rewarded and non-rewarded, respectively (Fig.~\ref{fig:stow}).
nodes.statement_short: Add $+1$ on reward and $-\omega$ on no reward to the played terminal.

nodes.name: Random-walk model parameters
nodes.statement: As shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:random}(a), $\alpha$ (right flight when rewarded) and $\beta$ (left flight when non-rewarded) are the parameters.

nodes.name: Machine A is better
nodes.statement: We assume that $P_A$ $>$ $P_B$ for simplicity.

nodes.name: Random-walk displacement
nodes.statement: After time step $t$, the displacement $R_k(t)$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) can be described by \begin{eqnarray} R_k(t) & = & \alpha (N_k - L_k) - \beta \hspace{1mm}L_k \nonumber \\ & = & \alpha N_k - (\alpha + \beta)\hspace{1mm}L_k . \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Parameter condition for correct judgment
nodes.statement: The overlapping area should decrease as $N_k$ increases so as to avoid incorrect judgments. This requirement can be expressed by the following forms: \begin{eqnarray} \alpha P_A - \beta (1 - P_A) & > & 0 , \\ \alpha P_B - \beta (1 - P_B) & < & 0 . \end{eqnarray} These expressions can be rearranged into the form \begin{equation} P_B < \frac{\beta}{\alpha + \beta} < P_A . \end{equation} In other words, the parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ must satisfy the above conditions so that the random walk correctly represents the larger judgment.
nodes.statement_short: For the random walk to separate the machines, $P_B < \beta/(\alpha+\beta) < P_A$.
assumptions: The overlapping area should decrease as $N_k$ increases so as to avoid incorrect judgments.
conclusions: the parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ must satisfy the above conditions so that the random walk correctly represents the larger judgment

nodes.name: Midpoint choice satisfies the conditions
nodes.statement: We can easily confirm that the following form satisfies the above conditions: \begin{equation} \frac{\beta}{\alpha + \beta} = \frac{P_A + P_B}{2} . \end{equation}
conclusions: the following form satisfies the above conditions

nodes.name: omega equals beta over alpha
nodes.statement: From $R_k(t)/\alpha $ $=$ $Q_k(t)$, we obtain $\omega = \frac{\beta}{\alpha}$.

nodes.name: Formula for omega_0
nodes.statement: From this and Eq.(\ref{eq:fixed}), we obtain \begin{eqnarray} \omega_0 & = & \frac{\gamma}{2 - \gamma} , \\ \gamma & = & P_A + P_B . \end{eqnarray} Here, we have set the parameter $\omega$ to $\omega_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Combining $\omega=\beta/\alpha$ with the midpoint choice gives $\omega_0=\gamma/(2-\gamma)$, $\gamma=P_A+P_B$.

nodes.name: TOW with omega_0 solves the MBP
nodes.statement: Therefore, we can conclude that the algorithm using the learning rule $Q_k$ with the parameter $\omega_0$ can solve the MBP correctly.
assumptions: the algorithm using the learning rule $Q_k$ with the parameter $\omega_0$

nodes.name: Imaginary system with known gamma
nodes.statement: On the other hand, in an imaginary circumstance in which the sum of the reward probabilities $\gamma$ $=$ $P_A$ $+$ $P_B$ is known to the player, we can update both of the two estimates simultaneously, even though only one of the machines was played.
nodes.statement_short: If $\gamma=P_A+P_B$ is known, both machines' estimates can be updated after each play.

nodes.name: Expected rewards Q'_k
nodes.statement: From the above estimates, each expected reward $Q^{\prime}_k$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) is given as follows: \begin{eqnarray} Q^{\prime}_A & = & N_A \hspace{1mm} \frac{N_A - L_A}{N_A} + N_B \hspace{1mm} \bigl( \gamma \hspace{1mm} - \frac{N_B - L_B}{N_B} \bigr) \nonumber \\ & = & N_A - L_A + (\gamma - 1) \hspace{1mm} N_B + L_B, \\ Q^{\prime}_B & = & N_A\hspace{1mm} \bigl( \gamma \hspace{1mm} - \frac{N_A - L_A}{N_A} \bigr) + N_B\hspace{1mm} \frac{N_B - L_B}{N_B} \nonumber \\ & = & N_B - L_B + (\gamma - 1) \hspace{1mm} N_A + L_A. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Expected rewards $Q'_A, Q'_B$ of the imaginary system computed from the table of estimates.

nodes.name: Transformed expected rewards Q''_j
nodes.statement: When we transform the expected rewards $Q^{\prime}_j$s into $Q^{\prime \prime}_j = Q^{\prime}_j / (2 - \gamma)$, we can obtain the difference \begin{equation} Q^{\prime \prime}_A - Q^{\prime \prime}_B = (N_A - N_B) - \frac{2}{2-\gamma} \hspace{1mm} (L_A - L_B). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Rescale $Q'_j$ by $1/(2-\gamma)$ and take the difference.

nodes.name: Coefficient match at omega_0
nodes.statement: Comparing the coefficients of Eq.(\ref{eq:dq}) and (\ref{eq:dqpp}), the differences in their constituent terms are always equal when $\omega=\omega_0$ (Eq.(\ref{eq:w0})) is satisfied. Eventually, we can obtain the nearly optimal weighting parameter $\omega_0$ in terms of $\gamma$.
conclusions: the differences in their constituent terms are always equal
nodes.statement_short: The TOW difference $Q_A-Q_B$ equals the imaginary system's $Q''_A-Q''_B$ exactly when $\omega=\omega_0$.

nodes.name: Equivalence of TOW learning rule and imaginary system
nodes.statement: This derivation implies that the learning rule for TOW dynamics is equivalent to that of the imaginary system in which both of the two estimates can be updated simultaneously. In other words, TOW dynamics imitates the imaginary system that determines its next move at time $t+1$ in referring to the estimates of the two machines, even if one of them was not actually played at time $t$.
conclusions: the learning rule for TOW dynamics is equivalent to that of the imaginary system in which both of the two estimates can be updated simultaneously
nodes.statement_short: TOW dynamics with $\omega_0$ behaves as if both machines' estimates were updated every step.

nodes.name: Origin of TOW performance
nodes.statement: This unique feature in the learning rule, derived from the fact that the sum of reward probabilities is given in advance, may be one of the origins of the high performance of TOW dynamics.

nodes.name: Near-optimality of omega_0 in simulations
nodes.statement: Monte Carlo simulations were performed it was verified that TOW dynamics with $\omega_0$ exhibits an exceptionally high performance, which is comparable to its peak performance---achieved with the optimal parameter $\omega_{opt}$.
nodes.statement_short: Simulations show TOW with $\omega_0$ performs close to its peak, attained at $\omega_{opt}$.

nodes.name: Deriving omega_opt
nodes.statement: To derive the optimal value $\omega_{opt}$ accurately, we need to take into account the fluctuation and other dynamics of terminals~\cite{kim4}.

nodes.name: omega_0 for M-machine case
nodes.statement: In addition, the essence of the process described here can be generalized to $M$-machine cases. To separate distributions of the top $m$-th and top $(m+1)$-th machine, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:random}(b), all we need is the following $\omega_0$: \begin{eqnarray} \omega_0 & = & \frac{\gamma^{\prime}}{2 - \gamma^{\prime}} , \\ \gamma^{\prime} & = & P_{(m)} + P_{(m+1)} \end{eqnarray} Here, $P_{(m)}$ denotes the top $m$-th reward probability.
conclusions: To separate distributions of the top $m$-th and top $(m+1)$-th machine, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:random}(b), all we need is the following $\omega_0$
nodes.statement_short: For $M$ machines, separating the $m$-th and $(m+1)$-th best uses $\omega_0=\gamma'/(2-\gamma')$ with $\gamma'=P_{(m)}+P_{(m+1)}$.

nodes.name: Cheater algorithm
nodes.statement: To further investigate the origins of the high performance of TOW dynamics, let us consider another imaginary model for solving the MBP, called the ``cheater algorithm.'' The cheater algorithm selects a machine to play according to the following estimate $S_k$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) \begin{eqnarray} S_A & = & X_{A, 1} + X_{A, 2}, + \cdots + X_{A, N} , \\ S_B & = & X_{B, 1} + X_{B, 2}, + \cdots + X_{B, N} . \end{eqnarray} Here, $X_{k, i}$ is a random variable that takes either $1$ (rewarded) or $0$ (non-rewarded). If $S_A$ $>$ $S_B$ at time $t=N$, machine $A$ is played at time $t=N+1$. If $S_B$ $>$ $S_A$ at time $t=N$, machine $B$ is played at time $t=N+1$. If $S_A$ $=$ $S_B$ at time $t=N$, a machine is played randomly at time $t=N+1$. Note that the algorithm refers to results of both machines at time $t$ without any attention to which machine was played at time $t-1$. In other words, the algorithm ``cheats'' because it plays both machines and collects both results, but declares that it plays only one machine at a time.
nodes.statement_short: Imaginary MBP algorithm that sums rewards of both machines every step and plays the one with the larger sum.

nodes.name: Compute reward sums
nodes.statement: The cheater algorithm selects a machine to play according to the following estimate $S_k$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) \begin{eqnarray} S_A & = & X_{A, 1} + X_{A, 2}, + \cdots + X_{A, N} , \\ S_B & = & X_{B, 1} + X_{B, 2}, + \cdots + X_{B, N} . \end{eqnarray} Here, $X_{k, i}$ is a random variable that takes either $1$ (rewarded) or $0$ (non-rewarded).
nodes.statement_short: Sum the 0/1 rewards of each machine over $N$ steps.

nodes.name: Play A if S_A larger
nodes.statement: If $S_A$ $>$ $S_B$ at time $t=N$, machine $A$ is played at time $t=N+1$.

nodes.name: Play B if S_B larger
nodes.statement: If $S_B$ $>$ $S_A$ at time $t=N$, machine $B$ is played at time $t=N+1$.

nodes.name: Random tie-break
nodes.statement: If $S_A$ $=$ $S_B$ at time $t=N$, a machine is played randomly at time $t=N+1$.

nodes.name: Mean and variance of rewards
nodes.statement: The expected value and the variance of $X_k$ are defined as $E (X_k) = \mu_k $ and $V (X_k) = \sigma_k^{2}$. Here, $\mu_k$ is the same as the $P_k$ defined earlier.

nodes.name: Gaussian approximation of S_k (cheater)
nodes.statement: From the central-limit theorem, $S_k$ has a Gaussian distribution with $E (S_k) = \mu_k N$ and $V (S_k) = \sigma_k^{2} N$.
conclusions: $S_k$ has a Gaussian distribution with $E (S_k)  =  \mu_k N$ and $V (S_k)  =  \sigma_k^{2} N$

nodes.name: Distribution of S = S_A - S_B (cheater)
nodes.statement: If we define a new variable $S = S_A - S_B$, $S$ has a Gaussian distribution and carries the following values: \begin{eqnarray} E (S) & = & (\mu_A + \mu_B) N ,\\ V (S) & = & (\sigma_A^{2} + \sigma_B^{2}) N ,\\ \sigma (S) & = & \sqrt{ \sigma_A^{2} + \sigma_B^{2}} \sqrt{N} . \end{eqnarray}
assumptions: we define a new variable $S = S_A - S_B$
conclusions: $S$ has a Gaussian distribution and carries the following values:
nodes.statement_short: The difference $S=S_A-S_B$ is Gaussian with mean and variance linear in $N$.

nodes.name: Probability of playing the worse machine
nodes.statement: From Fig.~\ref{fig:Qfunc}, the probability of playing machine $B$, which has a lower reward probability, can be described as {\bf Q}$(\frac{E(S)}{\sigma(S)})$.

nodes.name: Q-function
nodes.statement: Here, {\bf Q}$(x)$ is a {\bf Q}-function.

nodes.name: Cheater probability of playing B
nodes.statement: We obtain \begin{eqnarray} P(t=N+1,B) & = & {\bf Q}(\phi \sqrt{N}) . \end{eqnarray} Here, $\phi = \frac{\mu_A - \mu_B}{\sqrt{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2}}$.
nodes.statement_short: The cheater plays the worse machine at step $N+1$ with probability $Q(\phi\sqrt N)$.

nodes.name: Regret
nodes.statement: Using the Chernoff bound ${\bf Q}(x) \leq \frac{1}{2} \exp(-\frac{x^2}{2})$, we can calculate the upper bound of a measure, called the ``regret'', which quantifies the accumulated losses of the cheater algorithm.

nodes.name: Cheater regret is constant
nodes.statement: Note that the regret becomes constant as $N$ increases.
nodes.statement_short: Using the Chernoff bound, the cheater's expected number of bad plays is at most $1/2+1/\phi^2$.

nodes.name: TOW reward estimates S_k
nodes.statement: In this case, \begin{eqnarray} S_A & = & X_{A, 1} + X_{A, 2}, + \cdots + X_{A, N_A} - \omega L_A , \\ S_B & = & X_{B, 1} + X_{B, 2}, + \cdots + X_{B, N_B} - \omega L_B . \end{eqnarray} $X_{k, i}$ is also a random variable that takes either $1$ (rewarded) or $0$ (non-rewarded).
nodes.statement_short: TOW estimates: reward sums of each machine minus $\omega$ times its punishments.

nodes.name: Punishment count approximation
nodes.statement: Here, we use $L_k$$=$$(1 - \mu_k) N_k$.

nodes.name: Moments of S_k (TOW)
nodes.statement: Then, we obtain $E (S_k) = \{ \mu_k - (1 - \mu_k) \omega \} N_k$ and $V (S_k) = \sigma_k^{2} N_k$.

nodes.name: Moments of S (TOW)
nodes.statement: Using the new variables $S = S_A - S_B$, $N = N_A + N_N$, and $D = N_A - N_N$, we also obtain \begin{eqnarray} E (S) & = & \frac{\mu_A - \mu_B}{2} (1 + \omega) N + \nonumber \\ & & \{ \frac{\mu_A + \mu_B}{2} (1 + \omega) - \omega \} D ,\\ V (S) & = & \frac{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2}{2} N + \frac{\sigma_A^2 - \sigma_B^2}{2} D . \end{eqnarray}
assumptions: Using the new variables $S = S_A - S_B$, $N = N_A + N_N$, and $D = N_A - N_N$
nodes.statement_short: Mean and variance of $S=S_A-S_B$ for TOW in terms of $N$ and $D=N_A-N_B$.

nodes.name: Probability of playing B for TOW with omega_0
nodes.statement: If the conditions $\omega = \omega_0$ and $\sigma_A = \sigma_B$ $\equiv \sigma$ are satisfied, we then obtain \begin{eqnarray} E (S) & = & \frac{\mu_A - \mu_B}{2} (1 + \omega_0) N ,\\ V (S) & = & {\sigma^2} N , \end{eqnarray} and \begin{eqnarray} P(t=N+1,B) & = & {\bf Q}(\phi_{T} \sqrt{N}) . \end{eqnarray} Here, $\phi_{T} = \frac{(\mu_A - \mu_B) (1 + \omega_0)}{2 \sigma}$.
nodes.statement_short: With $\omega=\omega_0$ and equal variances, the D-term vanishes and TOW plays B with probability $Q(\phi_T\sqrt N)$.

nodes.name: TOW regret is constant
nodes.statement: We can then calculate the upper bound of the regret for TOW dynamics \begin{eqnarray} E(N_B) & = & \Sigma_{t=0}^{N-1} {\bf Q}(\phi_{T} \sqrt{t}) \nonumber \\ & \leq & \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{\phi_{T}^2} \left( \exp(-\frac{\phi_{T}^2}{2}(N-1)) - 1 \right) \\ & \rightarrow & \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\phi_{T}^2} . \end{eqnarray} Note that the regret for TOW dynamics also becomes constant as $N$ increases.
conclusions: Note that the regret for TOW dynamics also becomes constant as $N$ increases.
nodes.statement_short: TOW's expected number of worse-machine plays is bounded by $1/2+1/\phi_T^2$, so its regret is constant in $N$.

nodes.name: Logarithmic regret of optimal MBP algorithms
nodes.statement: It is known that optimal algorithms for the MBP, defined by Auer et al., have a regret proportional to $\log(N)$.
conclusions: optimal algorithms for the MBP, defined by Auer et al., have a regret proportional to $\log(N)$

nodes.name: Meaning of constant regret
nodes.statement: The regret has no finite upper bound as $N$ increases because it continues to require playing the lower-reward machine to ensure that the probability of incorrect judgment goes to zero. A constant regret means that the probability of incorrect judgment remains non-zero in TOW dynamics, although this probability is nearly equal to zero.
nodes.statement_short: Log regret keeps exploring so errors vanish; TOW's constant regret leaves a tiny nonzero error probability.

nodes.name: Practical suitability of TOW
nodes.statement: However, it would appear that the reward probabilities change frequently in actual decision-making situations, and their long-term behavior is not crucial for many practical purposes. For this reason, TOW dynamics would be more suited to real-world applications.
